extracted.intended_audience: general readers; students, educators, researchers, and journalists
extracted.subtask_description: An encyclopedic overview of plagiarism covering definitions, institutional policies, forms, detection methods, sanctions, educational responses, and the impact of technology (including AI). Intended to summarize standards and debates across academia, journalism, and the arts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of plagiarism
rubrics_metrics.description: "Plagiarism is the representation of another person's language, thoughts, ideas, or expressions as one's own original work."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Precise definitions vary by institution; the core element is passing off another's words/ideas as one's own. Contexts where originality is expected are central to the definition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Academic dishonesty and sanctions
rubrics_metrics.description: Within academia, plagiarism is considered academic dishonesty or academic fraud and offenders are subject to academic censure, up to and including expulsion for students and termination of contracts for professors and researchers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sanctions range from failing grades to suspension, expulsion, termination, loss of credibility, retraction of research papers; cases are typically heard by internal disciplinary committees. Severity may depend on repetition and seriousness (e.g., purchasing an assignment).

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal status vs moral/ethical offense
rubrics_metrics.description: Plagiarism as such 'does not exist in a legal sense' and is not specifically mentioned in current criminal or civil statutes, although related acts can implicate fraud, unfair competition, moral-rights violations, or torts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because plagiarism is primarily an ethical/moral breach rather than a statutory offense, remedies often come from institutional discipline or separate legal claims (e.g., copyright, contract). A common practical guideline: 'if you did not write it yourself; you must give credit.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction from copyright infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: Plagiarism and copyright infringement functionally overlap but are not equivalent concepts; plagiarism concerns false claims of authorship and undeserved credit, whereas copyright infringement concerns legal rights of the copyright holder.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An act can be plagiarism without infringing copyright, and vice versa; different standards and remedies apply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional definitions and variations
rubrics_metrics.description: Different universities and institutions define plagiarism in different terms (examples given: Stanford, Yale, Princeton, Brown, U.S. Naval Academy).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Stanford — 'use, without giving reasonable and appropriate credit...'; Yale — 'use of another's work, words, or ideas without attribution' including paraphrasing too close to original; Princeton — emphasizes 'deliberate' use. Institutions vary on emphasis (intentionality, scope of what counts, self-plagiarism).

rubrics_metrics.name: List of common forms of academic plagiarism (Turnitin's 10 forms)
rubrics_metrics.description: A survey identified 10 main forms students commit: submitting someone's work as their own; self-plagiarism; re-writing without citation; using quotations without citation; interweaving sources without citing; citing some but not all necessary passages; melding cited and uncited sections; 'close paraphrasing' (proper citations but wording too close); inaccurate citation; over-reliance on others' work with insufficient original thought.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This enumeration is used by educators to recognize varied behaviors beyond verbatim copying; each form may require different detection and pedagogical responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Four-level typology of plagiarism (lexis/syntax/semantics/ideas)
rubrics_metrics.description: A typology categorizes plagiarism according to the layer affected: characters-preserving (verbatim copying), syntax-preserving (synonym substitution), semantics-preserving (translation, paraphrase), and idea-preserving (appropriation of ideas or structures, reuse of text structure).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This typology helps detect and conceptualize non-verbatim forms of plagiarism (e.g., translation plagiarism or structural appropriation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rogeting (synonym-substitution evasion)
rubrics_metrics.description: The practice of modifying a published source by substituting synonyms for sufficient words to fool plagiarism-detection software ('Rogeting').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Described as an evolving anti-pattern; can create meaningless phrasing and is an attempt to evade text-matching tools rather than address attribution/understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contract cheating and ghostwriting
rubrics_metrics.description: Plagiarism can include 'contract cheating' where students pay someone else (essay mills) to do their work and ghostwriting where another writes for the author.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As of 2021, few jurisdictions prohibit operation/promotion of contract-cheating services; such acts are often treated as severe academic misconduct and may incur strong sanctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factors influencing students' decisions to plagiarize
rubrics_metrics.description: Studies identify predictors such as academic procrastination, perceived benefit of plagiarizing, availability/opportunity, heavy workloads, weak understanding of citation, and internalized social norms about plagiarism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Higher perceived sanctions and internalization of anti-plagiarism norms reduce incidence; teacher/task design can influence rates (e.g., monotonous tasks, heavy workload raise risk).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sanctions consistency and tariff approaches
rubrics_metrics.description: There is historical concern about inconsistent penalties across institutions; initiatives like a plagiarism tariff (UK, 2008) attempted to standardize responses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Penalty severity often calibrated to repetition and severity (e.g., purchased assignment → suspension/expulsion); institutions may differ in whether they consider ignorance a mitigating factor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Faculty strategies for detecting plagiarism
rubrics_metrics.description: Faculty use careful reading for inconsistencies in writing, note citation errors, use plagiarism-prevention education, and sometimes manually inspect suspicious papers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Not all instructors use text-matching software; manual reading can fail to detect plagiarism from unfamiliar sources; prevention education is emphasized alongside detection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plagiarism-detection systems (Turnitin) — functionality and limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Turnitin provides formative and summative assessments, uses adaptive AI (Turnitin Scoring Engine) to evaluate writing, highlights matching sentences, and assesses readability/genre familiarity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limitations: language and digital-footprint biases (small-language material less supported), privacy/copyright concerns from aggregating student work, lack of a single clear definition of plagiarism in reports, potential for differing instructor interpretations of similarity reports, and risk of over-reliance on technology for grading. The article flags that PDS may deter rather than definitively detect plagiarism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plagiarism education and pedagogical responses
rubrics_metrics.description: Educational responses include orientation, required writing courses, honor codes, prevention education, formative feedback, and staff development on plagiarism pedagogy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommended actions to reduce plagiarism: coordinate teaching to reduce student load, design tasks requiring original thought, reduce memorization emphasis, increase practical/individual activities, emphasize learning over punishment, and warn students about penalties. Education should extend to academic staff.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impact of the internet and information accessibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Easy access to information and copy-paste functionality have simplified copying from the web; empirical surveys report notable rates of admitted copying among students.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While internet accessibility correlates with plagiarism, some studies show medium (electronic vs. paper) does not necessarily increase plagiarism. Digital era increases need for teaching correct attribution for electronic sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impact of artificial intelligence and LLMs
rubrics_metrics.description: Generative AI (e.g., GPT-3, ChatGPT) can produce coherent text used to commit plagiarism; the rise of LLMs sparked debate about detection, pedagogy, and the possibility of widespread automated content generating a 'Plagiarism Singularity.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detectors like GPTZero have been introduced; debates range from calls to ban to proposals to teach with AI. AI complicates detection and raises new ethical/educational considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-plagiarism (text recycling/duplicate publication)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reusing significant, identical, or nearly identical portions of one's own work without acknowledgment is described as self-plagiarism or recycling fraud; Roig and others classify types: duplicate publication, salami-slicing, text recycling, and copyright infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Self-plagiarism is contested (some call it oxymoronic). Factors that may excuse reuse (Pamela Samuelson): restating previous work to set up new contribution; repeating portions for new evidence/arguments; different audience; or trivial reasons. Copyright transfer may complicate reuse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Codes of ethics & organizational policies on plagiarism/self-plagiarism
rubrics_metrics.description: Some journals and professional organizations explicitly address self-plagiarism (e.g., Journal of International Business Studies, ACM); others (e.g., APSA) do not specifically reference it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policies vary widely; authors should consult disciplinary/journal/organizational codes for expectations and disclosure requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reverse plagiarism (attribution without copying)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reverse plagiarism or 'attribution without copying' refers to falsely giving authorship credit to someone who did not author the work, or falsely claiming a source supports an assertion it does not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Though rarer, it occurs in similar contexts as traditional plagiarism and is treated as a form of misattribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Artistic appropriation vs plagiarism in the arts
rubrics_metrics.description: In the arts, practices such as imitation, pastiche, parody, collage, and appropriation complicate distinctions; 'there is no rigorous and precise distinction between imitation, stylistic plagiarism, copy, replica and forgery.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultural and historical norms affect acceptability; some appropriation is canonical in art history, but publishing another's art as one's own (art theft) is condemned, especially online.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical and power-dynamic critiques of detection tools
rubrics_metrics.description: Plagiarism-detection tools can create adversarial teacher–student dynamics, place students under surveillance, and may promote 'Western writing values' globally according to critiques.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Educators should weigh the deterring benefits against harms (fear, anxiety, cultural imposition) and emphasize pedagogy and clear definitions rather than airtight surveillance alone.
